bib.title: Cross-Validation and Cp Estimates of Prediction Error (Chapter 12, Computer Age Statistical Inference)

question: Having chosen a prediction rule, how do we estimate its predictive accuracy, nonparametrically (cross-validation) and by model-based covariance penalties (Cp, AIC, SURE)?
contributions: Define prediction error, apparent error and validation estimates
Covariance penalty lemma unifying Cp, AIC, SURE and bootstrap penalties
Ephemeral predictors warning for validation sets

results.claim: Apparent R^2 of 0.816 on the supernova fit falls to 0.701 once cross-validated error replaces apparent error.

results.claim: Apparent R^2 on supernova data before correction.

results.setup: Kidney data, B=1000 parametric bootstrap

limits: Err_cv estimates average algorithm error, not the error of the specific fitted rule (correlation with true Err is weak/negative in simulation).
Choosing the best rule by Err_cv is not itself cross-validated, so the minimum is optimistic.
Cp estimate for the lasso p=7 does not account for data-based selection of p.
Validation sets close in time to training data overstate accuracy (ephemeral predictors; Google Flu Trends).
Covariance penalty methods need a probability model; sigma^2 assumed known.
Minus signs are lost in the text layer: Table 12.1 values, eq 12.84 episode means (2 vs -2), and the sign of the 0.175 correlation are unconfirmed.
practices: Correct apparent error for rule fitting using cross-validation or a Cp-type penalty (12.2, 12.3).
Prefer grouped J-fold CV (J about 10) over leave-one-out for discontinuous rules, optionally averaged over splits (12.2, 12.5).
Use covariance penalty estimates over CV when a believable parametric model exists (12.3).
Use a validation set well separated in time or location from training data; block rather than random folds (12.4).
Beware that model selection by minimum CV error is not itself cross-validated (12.2).
